characters.name: Nils Fredrik Hallgren
characters.home: The comminister's house beside the church at Gamla Uppsala, in sight of the great royal mounds

identity.occupation: Comminister (assistant vicar) of Gamla Uppsala parish
identity.home: The comminister's house beside the church at Gamla Uppsala, in sight of the great royal mounds
identity.appearance: Gaunt and very upright, with white hair worn long at the collar, a clerical bib always spotless, and long cold fingers he folds over his hymnal.

drives.text: Root out the remnants of heathen belief in a parish that sits on the very graves of the old kings.
Hold the parish in the state church against the revivalist lay preachers who are emptying his pews.
Never again think about what he saw in the mound field when he was eleven.

voice.register: Measured, scriptural and chilly; quotes the catechism and the Bible as a matter of course, and never raises his voice.
mannerisms: Begins a reproach with 'I say this in love'
Glances towards the mounds when anyone mentions the old faith
Answers questions about folk belief with a question about churchgoing
sampleLines: I say this in love. The household examination is in March, and I shall expect the whole house, gentlefolk and servants alike.
The mounds are graves of heathen men, and graves are for the dead. I would thank you not to walk among them after dark.
There are those in this parish who would leave milk on a stone sooner than bring their children to be confirmed. You would not encourage them, I hope.

characters.background: Hallgren has served the parish of Gamla Uppsala for more than twenty years, long enough to have buried most of the farmers who were young when he came. He is conscientious, unbending and genuinely devoted to the souls in his charge, and he regards the lingering folk customs of his parish, the offerings at stones, the charms against the vittra, the summer fires, as a darkness he was sent to drive out. He also keeps the parish's household examination rolls, which record every person in every house, including who in the Society's household reads the catechism and who does not. As a boy, staying with an uncle at the parsonage, he walked into the mound field one autumn night and saw something there that he has spent his life calling a fever dream.

latentHooks.text: He has the Sight, suppressed since childhood; what he saw at the mounds was real, and he knows it.
He keeps the household examination rolls in exacting detail, noting not only catechism but rumours, absences and quarrels, for every farm in the parish.
He hopes to be made vicar of a better parish before he dies, and an archbishop's commendation for stamping out superstition would bring it.
Thirty years ago he quietly entered a foundling child in the register under a false parentage to spare a family's shame; the child grew up in the parish.

networkLinks.place: Gamla Uppsala and the cathedral chapter
networkLinks.nature: Comminister with the ear of the cathedral chapter
networkLinks.influence: Can denounce the Society's household from the pulpit, or bring the chapter's displeasure on any household it favours.

networkLinks.nature: Fellow-sceptic and churchgoer
networkLinks.influence: Can pass the constable what he learns at the examinations.

networkLinks.nature: Confidant of the pious manor families of the district
networkLinks.influence: Can make the Society's members unwelcome at the local manors.

characters.attitudeReason: He suspects the Society of indulging the old superstitions his life has been spent driving out, and fears what they might make him remember.

characters.name: Karl Edvard Hägg
characters.home: Two rooms above a harness-maker's in Svartbäcken, Uppsala

identity.occupation: Senior police constable of the Uppsala town police
identity.home: Two rooms above a harness-maker's in Svartbäcken, Uppsala
identity.appearance: Broad and slightly stooped, grey side-whiskers clipped short, a uniform coat brushed thin at the elbows, and a notebook he writes in with a carpenter's pencil.

drives.text: Keep cunning folk, spiritualists and confidence men from preying on frightened country people.
Have Uppsala's books balanced at the end of each month: every report filed, every drunk accounted for.
Reach his pension without a scandal that would let the stadsfiskal pass him over.

voice.register: Plain, slow and official; Uppland country speech under a policeman's formal phrases.
mannerisms: Writes down what you say before he answers it
Calls everyone by their full name and parish
Ends a question with a long silence instead of a second question
sampleLines: I'll have that again, slowly. Where were you on the evening of the fourteenth, and who will swear to it?
I've seen a widow in Bälinge sell her last cow to a man who promised to talk to her drowned boy. I don't care for gentlemen who see what others can't.
Nothing in Uppsala walks at night that can't be put in the cells by morning, sir. That is my experience.

characters.background: Hägg was born a farmhand's son at Vaksala, served eight years in the Uppland regiment and joined the town police when it was little more than a watch. He is honest to the point of rudeness and has never taken a coin. Fifteen years ago he arrested a travelling 'wise man' who had stripped a parish of its savings by promising to lift curses, and he watched the widow at the heart of that case hang herself in her barn before the trial. He has distrusted anyone who trades in the unseen ever since. He has heard that a group of gentlefolk near Gamla Uppsala receive strange letters from the countryside and travel out to answer them, and to him that sounds like the same trade in better clothes.

latentHooks.text: He found the widow in Bälinge alive enough to speak, and what she told him about her son's drowning is not in his report; it did not fit.
His wife's brother runs a tavern in Fjärdingen without a proper licence, and Hägg has been looking the other way for years.
Every Sunday afternoon he copies the week's incidents into a private ledger he keeps at home, with notes he would never put in an official report.
The post of police sergeant (överkonstapel) falls vacant next year, and a clean, celebrated arrest would win it.

networkLinks.nature: Senior constable, trusted by the stadsfiskal for country errands
networkLinks.influence: Can have the Society's names noted as persons of interest, or quietly ask a rural länsman to refuse them help.

networkLinks.nature: Knows the parish clerks who keep the registers
networkLinks.influence: Can learn who moved into and out of a parish, and when, before the Society can.

networkLinks.nature: Fellow-sceptic; they compare notes after church
networkLinks.influence: Each feeds the other's suspicions about the Society.

characters.attitudeReason: He believes the Society are well-born charlatans of the kind he has seen ruin poor families, and he is waiting for them to make a mistake.

characters.name: Henrik Ekelund
characters.home: Rented rooms on Övre Slottsgatan, Uppsala, crammed with notebooks and dialect word-slips

identity.occupation: Docent (lecturer) in Nordic languages at Uppsala University
identity.home: Rented rooms on Övre Slottsgatan, Uppsala, crammed with notebooks and dialect word-slips
identity.appearance: Tall and thin, with spectacles pushed up into untidy fair hair, a velvet waistcoat with a burn hole, and pockets full of folded paper slips.

drives.text: Compile the definitive record of Swedish folk belief, parish by parish, before the railway and the emigrant ships erase it.
Win the chair that his rival in Lund is also courting.
Find out, privately, whether any of it is true.

voice.register: Eager, learned and digressive; drops into dialect words with delight and corrects his own Latin.
mannerisms: Writes words on slips of paper mid-conversation
Asks how a thing is said in your home parish
sampleLines: In Hälsingland they don't say she was taken, they say she was 'borrowed'. Borrowed! Do you hear the difference? It means someone expects her back.
I am a man of science, naturally. But if you were to go to that mill on Midsummer Eve, would you be so kind as to take me with you?
Professor Tornell would call this peasant fancy. Professor Tornell has never sat in a cowshed in Orsa at four in the morning.

characters.background: Ekelund is a pastor's son from Dalarna who escaped into philology and has never quite come back down. In 1872 he helped a circle of students found one of the new dialect societies, the landsmålsföreningar, which send young men out every summer to write down the speech, songs and tales of their home provinces. His rooms are a paper flood of word-slips, transcribed charms and folk tunes. He tells his colleagues that folk belief is a fossil record of the Nordic mind; he has privately begun to suspect it is also a field report. He has worked out that the Society knows more than it says and is courting them shamelessly.

latentHooks.text: His student collectors spread across half the provinces every summer, and their notebooks often record strange events weeks before the papers do.
Last spring, alone in his rooms, he tried one of the charms he had transcribed, and something answered; he has not slept well since.
He borrowed a seventeenth-century manuscript of spells from the university library's closed collection and has not returned it.
He dreams of a learned paper on 'a living tradition of seers near Uppsala', which would make his name and expose the Society.

networkLinks.nature: Docent with friends among the younger faculty and the student nations
networkLinks.influence: Can open the library's closed collections and the university's archives, or a word from him can get the Society's members barred from them.

networkLinks.nature: Corresponds with dozens of country vicars who send him local customs
networkLinks.influence: Can find out quickly which parish has had strange deaths or customs revived.

networkLinks.nature: Writes popular articles on folk belief for the papers
networkLinks.influence: Can make a case into a learned curiosity in print, for better or worse.

characters.attitudeReason: He sees the Society as the most exciting source he has ever found and wants their trust, and their secrets.

characters.name: Johan August Blom
characters.home: The newspaper office and flat above it on Drottninggatan, Uppsala, smelling of ink and wet paper

identity.occupation: Editor and part-owner of the liberal newspaper Fyrisposten
identity.home: The newspaper office and flat above it on Drottninggatan, Uppsala, smelling of ink and wet paper
identity.appearance: Heavy-set and red-cheeked, with a magnificent brown beard, a cigar he rarely lights, and shirt cuffs grey with printer's ink.

drives.text: Keep the paper's subscribers ahead of the conservative rival across the river.
Push the cause of reform: schools, railways, an end to superstition and to the clergy's grip on the countryside.
Get the true story of what the Society does, whatever it is, and print it first.

voice.register: Booming, jovial and argumentative; speaks in headlines and leading articles even across a dinner table.
mannerisms: Taps the table with a folded newspaper to make a point
Calls everyone 'my friend' especially when he disagrees
Repeats a good phrase twice to remember it for print
sampleLines: My friend, the age of trolls is over. The age of the telegraph is here. Superstition in the countryside, that's the headline, that's the story.
You've been to Hedesunda twice this month. I don't ask why. I merely note it. I am a noting sort of man.
Give me something true and I'll print it straight. Give me nothing and I shall have to print what people say, and people say such things.

characters.background: Blom was a schoolteacher in Västerås until a sharp article on the cathedral chapter cost him his post. He drifted into journalism in Stockholm, came to Uppsala to run Fyrisposten in 1864, and has turned a dull advertiser into a lively, quarrelsome liberal paper read in every coffee house in town. He mocks rural superstition in print as a matter of policy, but he is too good a newspaperman not to notice that certain country stories keep ending with the arrival of the same gentlefolk from Gamla Uppsala. He does not yet know whether the Society are a story about fraud, about science, or about something else.

latentHooks.text: He pays small sums to servants, coachmen and telegraph clerks for news, and some of them work close to the Society.
A libel suit from a Uppsala alderman is pending, and losing it would ruin him; he would trade a great deal for leverage.
His younger sister has been in the asylum at Uppsala for ten years after seeing 'the woman in the lake'; he visits her monthly and tells no one.
He means to stand for the second chamber of the Riksdag, and a sensational exposé would make his name across the county.

networkLinks.nature: Editor with correspondents in the provincial papers
networkLinks.influence: Can put a story in print across the county within the week, praising or mocking the Society.

networkLinks.nature: Drinks with junior constables who sell him the night's arrests
networkLinks.influence: Can learn of the Society's dealings with the police almost as soon as they happen.

networkLinks.nature: Buys road gossip from Brita Strand
networkLinks.influence: Learns who has been coming and going from the Society's headquarters.

characters.attitudeReason: Neither friend nor foe; the Society is a story he has not yet decided how to write.

characters.name: Brita Strand
characters.home: Strands gästgivargård, by the post road a short walk from the Society's headquarters

identity.occupation: Keeper of the coaching inn (gästgivaregård) on the northern road out of Uppsala
identity.home: Strands gästgivargård, by the post road a short walk from the Society's headquarters
identity.appearance: Small and quick, with ink-stained fingers from the post ledger, a black silk widow's cap worn rakishly, and a loud laugh that carries across the yard.

drives.text: Keep the inn and its post-horse contract out of the hands of her late husband's cousin, who wants it.
Know every traveller's business before they have unbuckled their bags.
See her daughter Lovisa married to someone with prospects, not the stable lad she keeps looking at.

voice.register: Warm, fast and mercantile; switches to careful politeness for gentlefolk and back again the moment they leave.
mannerisms: Calls regular guests by what they drink
Lowers her voice for the interesting parts and raises it for the rest
sampleLines: A room is one riksdaler, the horses are extra, and your secrets, my dear, are free. I'll only charge you for keeping them.
Three of you came back in the small hours on Tuesday, muddy to the knees, and not one word to old Brita. I'm hurt.
The post coach from Gävle had a lady on it who asked after your house by name. I told her nothing, naturally. Well. Very little.

characters.background: Brita married into the inn at nineteen and ran it in practice long before her husband drank himself into the churchyard in 1866. The inn holds the county contract to keep post-horses for travellers, which makes it a nerve of the district: coachmen, pedlars, emigrants on their way to the Gothenburg boats and commercial travellers all pass through her taproom, and she forgets nothing. She likes the Society because they pay promptly, bring interesting guests and never quibble over the bill, but she has noticed that trouble follows them up the road, and she charges accordingly.

latentHooks.text: Her husband died owing money to his cousin Anders Strand, a grain merchant in Uppsala, who holds a note on the inn and could call it in.
She keeps the post-horse ledger meticulously, so she can say who hired horses for which road, and when, going back twenty years.
One winter night years ago she gave shelter to a traveller who left before dawn and was never seen again; she kept his trunk, and something in it frightens her.
Every coachman and post-boy between Uppsala and Gävle drinks at her bar and carries her gossip.

networkLinks.nature: Feeds and lodges the timber and railway companies' men on the road north
networkLinks.influence: Can learn when company agents travel and where, and can make a stranger's stay pleasant or very uncomfortable.

networkLinks.nature: Sells the editor small items of news for a few skilling
networkLinks.influence: Can put a story about the Society into the paper, or keep one out of it, with a word.

networkLinks.nature: Elin Alm's aunt by marriage; Elin visits on her free Sundays
networkLinks.influence: Hears, sooner or later, most of what goes on in the headquarters' kitchen.

characters.attitudeReason: Good customers who pay on time and bring interesting company, though she suspects they are worth more than they pay.

characters.name: Elin Alm
characters.home: A small room behind the kitchen at the Society's headquarters near Gamla Uppsala

identity.occupation: Maid of all work at the Society's headquarters
identity.home: A small room behind the kitchen at the Society's headquarters near Gamla Uppsala
identity.appearance: Sturdy and freckled, with red, chapped hands, a plaited fair braid pinned under a cap, and very sharp grey eyes that miss nothing.

drives.text: Save enough for a steerage passage to join her brother Per in Minnesota.
Keep the household she serves safe from the things she has seen in the yard at night.
Honour what her grandmother taught her without the vicar finding out.

voice.register: Quiet and correct with the gentlefolk, broad Hälsingland dialect when frightened or among her own.
mannerisms: Answers a question with 'if the master wishes'
Touches the iron nail sewn into her apron hem when she is uneasy
Goes very still and listens before she speaks
sampleLines: If the master wishes. Only, I'd not leave the stable door open after dark this week. Not this week.
My grandmother used to put a pair of scissors under the cradle. I don't hold with such things, of course. But I've put a pair under the back step.
Someone was asking at the inn what time the gentlemen come and go. I didn't care for the look of him.

characters.background: Elin came south from a croft near Bollnäs after the famine of 1868 took her parents and sent her brother to America. Her grandmother was a respected wise woman who could stop blood and find lost cattle, and taught Elin far more than either of them ever told the vicar. She came to the headquarters through her aunt's connection with the inn and was hired because she did not scream on her first night. She half-has the Sight herself, keeps the house's old protections quietly in order, and is fiercely loyal, but she is also saving every coin she can, and coins come from more than one direction.

latentHooks.text: Editor Blom pays her a few skilling for harmless news of the household; she tells herself she gives him nothing that matters.
She keeps her grandmother's book of charms and remedies, written in a mixture of Swedish and old rune-signs, hidden in her trunk.
Letters from Per in Minnesota arrive irregularly through the inn; one has not come in five months, and she fears the worst.
She sometimes sees what the Society sees, and does not yet know whether to tell them.

networkLinks.nature: Niece by marriage; visits on free Sundays
networkLinks.influence: Can pass word to or from the inn, and anything she says there travels.

networkLinks.nature: Paid, occasional informant
networkLinks.influence: Can, without meaning harm, let slip the Society's movements to the press.

networkLinks.nature: Communicant who must attend the household examination
networkLinks.influence: Her answers at the catechism examination can draw the vicar's attention to the house.

characters.attitudeReason: Loyal to the household that took her in and frightened for it, though she keeps her own counsel and her own savings.

characters.name: Gustaf Adolf Nordenfelt

identity.occupation: Professor of medicine at Uppsala University and physician to the academic hospital
identity.home: A tall stone house on Trädgårdsgatan, Uppsala
identity.appearance: Narrow, silver-whiskered, immaculate black coat, a gold pince-nez he polishes when contradicted.

drives.text: Prove that every so-called haunting is nerves, hunger or bad air, and make the lesson public.
Protect his standing on the university board and the asylum committee.

voice.register: Dry, precise, condescending academic Swedish with Latin tags.
sampleLines: Superstition is merely a diagnosis that has not yet been made.
Bring me the patient and leave the spirits at the door.

characters.background: Trained in Paris and Vienna, he built his name on the study of hysteria in country parishes. He has quietly read the Society's cases as source material and considers its members interesting patients rather than colleagues.

latentHooks.text: He is drafting a treatise on 'collective delusion in the Uppland peasantry' and would like the Society's members as unwitting case studies.
Years ago he signed a death certificate for a patient with a cause that he knew was false, to avoid an inquiry into a colleague.
He sits on the asylum committee and can open or close the ward doors where Editor Blom's sister lies.

networkLinks.nature: Senior professor and board member
networkLinks.influence: Can discredit the Society's claims to scholars and can grant or refuse access to the university library.

networkLinks.nature: Mentor to many district physicians
networkLinks.influence: District doctors send him their odd cases and follow his reading of them.

characters.attitudeReason: He regards the Society as a symptom of the age's credulity and wants proof of that.

relationships.nature: Mutual wariness; the professor has twice been needled in print
Disapproving senior colleague
Buys medical books from her and distrusts her stock

characters.name: Sofia Wennerberg

identity.occupation: Antiquarian bookseller and dealer in old manuscripts
identity.home: A narrow shop with rooms above on Fyristorg, Uppsala
identity.appearance: Stout and quick-eyed, ink on her cuffs, a shawl always pinned with a brooch of dark amber.

drives.text: Keep the shop solvent and her late husband's name respectable.
Collect rare manuscripts of folk magic and sell them to the right buyers.

voice.register: Warm, chatty, a shopkeeper's flattery over a sharp mind.
mannerisms: Taps the spine of a book as she talks price
Lowers her voice for anything valuable
sampleLines: Everything has a price, my dear, but not everything has a buyer.
I never ask where a book has been, only what it will fetch.

characters.background: Widowed six years, she kept the shop going through the lean years by trading in what the university's collectors would not sell openly. She likes the Society because it buys books and asks interesting questions, and she is a little afraid of what some of her volumes contain.

latentHooks.text: She owes a large sum on her stock to a grain merchant in Uppsala and cannot easily meet the next instalment.
She quietly sells and lends seventeenth-century spell manuscripts to Docent Ekelund and to others who ask no questions.
One bundle of papers in her cellar came from a dead pastor's estate and names living families in a way that could shame them.

networkLinks.nature: Supplier to scholars and students
networkLinks.influence: Hears which professors are hunting which texts and can steer a student to a source.

characters.attitudeReason: The Society are good customers and make her shop feel like it matters.

relationships.nature: Valued customer and gossiping friend
Customer she finds tiresome
Old acquaintance who trades news over coffee

characters.name: Per-Olof Sjöberg

identity.occupation: Rural constable (länsman) of the Sala district
identity.home: The länsman's farm on the road north of Sala
identity.appearance: Heavy-shouldered, red-bearded, a cap he turns in his hands, boots always muddy.

drives.text: Keep the district quiet and his reports tidy so the county governor leaves him alone.
Get out from under the debt he owes the manor.

voice.register: Blunt, slow country speech, wary of towns and titles.
mannerisms: Answers a question with a question
Looks at the door when anyone mentions the manor
sampleLines: I report what I can put my hand on. The rest is for the vicar.
Folk talk. Folk always talk. Doesn't make it so.

characters.background: He has policed the Sala district for eleven years, where the silver mine has gone quiet and half the young men have left for America. He has seen things at night that he does not write down.

latentHooks.text: He borrowed money from the Baron at Salberga to cover his wife's illness and now cannot refuse the Baron a favour.
He once closed a death as 'drowned by accident' because the real circumstances would have sent a crofter's family to ruin.
He walks the old mine tracks alone at dusk, and never says why.

networkLinks.nature: Rural constable answering to the county governor
networkLinks.influence: Can open or close access to inquest papers and to any crime scene in the district.

networkLinks.nature: Debtor to the Baron
networkLinks.influence: Passes on word of strangers asking questions.

characters.attitudeReason: He distrusts anyone from Uppsala who arrives asking about local deaths.

relationships.nature: Exchanges terse letters; respects him cautiously
Debtor and reluctant servant
Resents the company engineer's airs

characters.name: Lovisa Hedman
characters.home: a croft near Delsbo in Hälsingland

identity.occupation: Midwife and healer, known as a cunning woman
identity.home: A grey timber croft near Delsbo, Hälsingland, with herbs hanging from the rafters
identity.appearance: Small and bent, hands like roots, a black headscarf and very pale eyes.

drives.text: Pass her remedies and the old rules to someone who will keep them before she dies.
Keep the vicar and the doctor from taking away her trade.

voice.register: Slow Hälsingland dialect, proverb-laden, speaks of the unseen as plain neighbours.
mannerisms: Answers questions sideways with a proverb
Spits lightly to the side after naming a bad thing
Never says 'thank you' for a gift
sampleLines: What you feed in the dark will come to your door in the light.
Ask politely and give something. That is all the old rules ever were.

characters.background: She has delivered half the parish and buried a good part of it. She keeps the old customs of offerings and thresholds, and she remembers the Society's founders from a hard winter long ago.

latentHooks.text: She knew Elin Alm's grandmother and once exchanged charms with her by letter.
She has never told the vicar that she leaves milk out each Thursday on the boundary stone of the croft.
She will not travel after dark and will not cross a running stream on certain days.

networkLinks.nature: Tolerated by the vicar, scorned by the church council
networkLinks.influence: Mothers in four parishes trust her over the district doctor.

networkLinks.nature: Rivalry with the district doctor over births
networkLinks.influence: Hears of sudden deaths and strange illnesses before the authorities do.

characters.attitudeReason: She sees the Society as heirs of people she once respected, and has not yet decided if they are worthy.

relationships.nature: Knew her grandmother and keeps a quiet interest in the girl
He calls her a witch from the pulpit stairs

characters.name: Carl Gustaf Gyllenhammar

identity.occupation: Baron, owner of Salberga manor and shares in the Sala silver works
identity.home: Salberga manor near Sala, a yellow wooden house with a mouldering park
identity.appearance: Tall, stooped, courtly, a faded uniform coat from his youth and a limp he hides.

drives.text: Save the estate from bankruptcy by any means that will not shame the name.
Learn whether the old bargains made by his family are still binding.

voice.register: Gracious, old-fashioned aristocratic Swedish with French words, charm that slips into pleading.
mannerisms: Says 'my dear sir' when he is afraid
Glances at the portrait of his grandfather
sampleLines: A gentleman's debts are matters of honour, and honour, alas, is expensive.
My family has always treated the land with respect. Some respect is costly.

characters.background: The last of his line, he inherited an estate with a mine that yields less every year and a family history of strange bargains. He welcomes the Society as helpers, but intends to use them to settle a private account.

latentHooks.text: His grandfather signed an agreement with something on the estate's land in exchange for the silver, and the Baron has found the paper.
He is mortgaged to the hilt to a Stockholm bank and has promised the mine to an investor he cannot satisfy.
He intends to have the Society remove, or silence, whatever haunts the old shaft so the company can reopen it.

networkLinks.nature: Old nobility with neighbours and tenants
networkLinks.influence: Can grant or deny access to land, tenants and records on the estate.

networkLinks.nature: Shareholder in the silver works
networkLinks.influence: Can open the mine records to the Society or lock them away.

characters.attitudeReason: He wants the Society's help and hides that he also wants to use it.

relationships.nature: Creditor and patron of the local constable
Uneasy partner in the plan to reopen the mine
Distant acquaintance through the archbishop's circle

characters.name: Matilda Forsberg

identity.occupation: Telegraph clerk at Uppsala railway station
identity.home: A rented attic room near the station, Uppsala
identity.appearance: Slight, sharp-chinned, ink-stained fingers, a tidy blue dress mended at the hem.

drives.text: Earn enough to bring her brother's family out of poverty or to follow him to America.
Be taken seriously in a post where men talk over her.

voice.register: Quick, clipped, telegraphic, with a clerk's habit of precision.
mannerisms: Taps on the counter in rhythm
Drops her voice when a message is private
sampleLines: A telegram is paid for by the word, so I learn which words matter.
I don't read them. I merely see them go by.

characters.background: She came from a crofter family in Roslagen and learned the telegraph through a pastor's patronage. She sees every message of every important person in Uppsala and tells herself she keeps quiet about them.

latentHooks.text: She passes snippets of telegrams to Editor Blom for a few riksdaler each, and has told herself it is harmless.
Her brother in Minnesota writes to her about a man from Uppland who carries a sickness the doctors there cannot name.
She copies unusual messages into a small notebook she keeps inside her stays.

networkLinks.nature: Paid informant to Editor Blom
networkLinks.influence: Can tell the Society what is being wired about them, and tell the press what the Society wires.

networkLinks.nature: Sends and receives constabulary telegrams
networkLinks.influence: Sees police inquiries before the Society does.

characters.attitudeReason: The Society's messages are the most interesting thing she handles, and they tip generously.

relationships.nature: Paid informant, uneasy about it
Friendly acquaintance; both wait for letters from America
He questions her about wires and she fears his glare

characters.name: Jonas Ryd

identity.occupation: Shoemaker and lay preacher of a free-church congregation
identity.home: A workshop and chapel room behind a tanner's yard in Gävle
identity.appearance: Lean, bright-eyed, a threadbare coat, hands stained with blacking and a battered Bible always at hand.

drives.text: Save souls from the state church's lukewarm faith and from the devil's tricks.
Expose anyone who deals with spirits as a servant of the enemy.

voice.register: Fervent preacher's cadence, scripture quoted as weapon, warmth turning into denunciation.
sampleLines: There is no neutral ground between the Lord and the spirits that whisper in the woods.
You carry the Sight as a gift? Brother, that is a snare.

characters.background: He has been fined twice for holding conventicles. He saw something as a boy that he has since called Satan, and he has devoted his life to denouncing anything that stirs the old world. He regards the Society as sorcerers.

latentHooks.text: The thing he saw as a boy was real, and he has never admitted to anyone that it spoke to him kindly.
His congregation includes mill-hands and dock workers who will gather at a word from him.
He hopes to be recognised as the leader of the free church in the province.

networkLinks.nature: Open adversary of the state clergy

Available.background: Hallgren has served the parish of Gamla Uppsala for more than twenty years, long enough to have buried most of the farmers who were young when he came. He is conscientious, unbending and genuinely devoted to the souls in his charge, and he regards the lingering folk customs of his parish, the offerings at stones, the charms against the vittra, the summer fires, as a darkness he was sent to drive out. He also keeps the parish's household examination rolls, which record every person in every house, including who in the Society's household reads the catechism and who does not. As a boy, staying with an uncle at the parsonage, he walked into the mound field one autumn night and saw something there that he has spent his life calling a fever dream.

She came to the headquarters through her aunt's connection with the inn and was hired because she did not scream on her first night. She half-has the Sight herself, keeps the house's old protections quietly in order, and is fiercely loyal, but she is also saving every coin she can, and coins come from more than one direction.
